label: Kofun period (burial mounds)
description: The Yayoi-Kofun transition; large burial mounds (kofun), haniwa (clay figurines), and bronze mirrors are the archaeological context for the later mythographic tradition [S17].

label: Yayoi-Kofun material culture
description: Iron tools, rice agriculture, and the emerging Yamato polity; the social world in which the kami-cults later codified in the Kojiki took shape [S17][S21].

label: Kojiki compiled
description: 'Records of Ancient Matters,' the earliest Japanese mythographic text, compiled under imperial order [S1].

label: Nihon Shoki compiled
description: 'Chronicles of Japan,' the second major mythographic/annalistic text [S2].

label: Engishiki (ritual code)
description: A Heian-era ritual and administrative code that records shrine rites and the institutional Shinto [S19].

label: Kitano Tenjin illustrated legends
description: Medieval illustrated (emakimono) accounts of deities and heroes, e.g. the Tenjin (Michizane) legends [S7].

label: Shinbutsu-gazurra and Edo-period deity imagery
description: Printed deity-compendium (shinbutsu-gazurra, e.g. Kanda Genbun's 1720 work) standardizing visual images of the kami [S13][S14].

label: Meiji Restoration; state Shinto
description: The Meiji state separates Shinto from Buddhism and constructs a state Shinto with the imperial line at its center, institutionalizing the Kojiki genealogy [S21].

label: Shrine ordinances (jinja rei)
description: State ordinances codifying shrine ranks and rites, further institutionalizing the mythographic tradition [S21].

label: Renunciation of divinity (humanity declaration)
description: The postwar declaration that the emperor and people are not of a divine origin, marking the end of the official divine-status framing [S21].
